📌 Rebase Tokens: Why Your Balance Can Change Without a Trade

Main Points
⏺ Some tokens automatically adjust holder balances through a rebase mechanism
⏺ Your token count can increase or decrease without a normal buy or sell
⏺ This post explains why “more tokens” doesn’t always mean “more money”

1️⃣ Core Idea — the protocol periodically recalculates balances, increasing or decreasing token amounts.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — to target a price, manage supply, or create a special monetary design.
3️⃣ The Trap — if your balance grows but price falls harder, you didn’t actually profit.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — exchanges, wallets, and DeFi protocols may not handle rebasing balances cleanly.
5️⃣ Practical Check — track your share of total supply, liquidity, and rebase rules, not just token count.

Final Thoughts

Rebase tokens change both price and quantity. Beginners see “more coins,” but the market prices real value.

What does “gas” mean in crypto? 

“Gas” is important in the world of crypto. Simply put, gas is the payment needed when making a transaction or interacting with a smart contract on a blockchain — i.e., the network fee you pay. 

Gas is usually paid in the given blockchain’s native cryptocurrency — e.g., ETH is used for transactions on Ethereum, and BNB is used for the same on BNB Smart Chain). These fees go to miners or validators responsible for keeping networks secure and confirming transactions. Gas fees also prevent spam on the network, keeping the blockchain running smoothly.

🤖Still Scared AI Is Coming For Your Job? 

Here's 20 Repos To Actually Do Something About It

1. Prompt-Engineering-Guide
Explains how to actually get useful, reliable output from AI models instead of guessing and hoping.

2. AI-For-Beginners
Covers the broader AI landscape, not just LLMs, so you're not caught off guard by the next big shift either.

3. generative-ai-for-beginners
A calm, lesson-by-lesson intro to building with generative AI, no ML background assumed.

4. anthropic-cookbook
Real code examples for building things with Claude, straight from the people who make it.

5. openai-cookbook
The same idea for OpenAI's models, practical patterns instead of theory.

6. ML-For-Beginners
Twelve weeks of classic machine learning basics, useful groundwork before jumping into AI specifically.

7. llama_index
Handles connecting AI models to your own data and documents, a skill that comes up constantly in real jobs now.

8. ollama
Lets you run AI models on your own machine, good for understanding them without relying on an API key.

9. llama.cpp
Shows what's actually happening when a model runs, right down to the hardware level.

10. transformers
The library behind most modern AI models, worth exploring even just to see how they're built.

11. awesome-ai-agents
A running list of AI agent projects and frameworks, handy for keeping track of a space that moves fast.

12. nanoGPT
A small, readable implementation of GPT, built by Andrej Karpathy so you can see the whole thing without getting lost. 

13. AutoGPT
One of the earliest autonomous AI agent projects, still useful for understanding how agents plan and act.

14. gpt-engineer
An AI agent that writes entire codebases from a prompt, worth trying just to see what it's actually capable of.

15. OpenHands
An open source AI coding agent, a good look at where AI-assisted development is heading.

16. awesome-machine-learning
A broad, well-organized list of ML resources and libraries across every language, a solid reference to keep bookmarked.

17. langchain
The most widely used framework for wiring AI models into actual applications, worth knowing even if you end up not using it.

18. Awesome-LLM
A curated list of papers, models, and tools, good for going deeper once the basics feel comfortable.

19. applied-ml
Real-world write-ups from companies on how they actually use ML and AI in production, not just in demos.

20. llm-course
A structured path from "what is an LLM" to actually fine-tuning and deploying one yourself.

🇮🇷☢️ Tehran’s Reply: Everything Is Fine. So Let’s Leave the Nuclear Treaty.

Iran’s response to Trump’s “Economic D-Day” rests on one claim: American pressure is proof of American weakness.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Trump’s announcement was a distraction from the United States’ own “unprecedented debt & surging interest costs.” He warned that “doubling down on failed policies” would bring Washington another defeat and harden Iranian hostility. He called U.S. pressure “economic terrorism” against the global economy and national sovereignty. 

Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi put the contradiction more bluntly. Washington, he said, claims Iran is near defeat and “hanging by a thread,” yet asks every ally to help defeat it. The military campaign failed, he argued, and Washington is now calling its next failure economic warfare.

Then came the parliamentary answer.

Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of parliament’s National Security Committee, said the “best response” to Trump’s escalation would be for Iran to leave the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. He said a withdrawal would require approval from Iran’s senior leadership. 

Iran may respond to economic pressure by leaving the legal framework it cites whenever Washington questions its nuclear program.

The committee’s chairman, Ebrahim Azizi, took a different line. He said Iran was monitoring U.S. moves closely and warned that another miscalculation would bring consequences “more severe than before.” He called for an end to the U.S. military presence in the region and for Washington to accept “Iran’s new regional order.”

The IRGC promised an upgrade. Its spokesman, Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi, said Iran is making its weapons more precise, more destructive, and more technologically advanced. If another war starts, he said, its weapons will be different from those used before — in warhead design, accuracy, range, or other capabilities. 

Those threats sit alongside a less heroic list of priorities.

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has put military reinforcement and food supplies on the same list. The pairing reflects a practical concern: inflation and shortages can erode a country’s ability to sustain a long conflict.

Former president Mohammad Khatami has warned against turning “wartime emotions” into a method of government.

On the ground, fuel shortages have reportedly shut some gas stations in Tehran, while drivers at others waited more than an hour to fill their tanks. At the Two Dolphins market in Dargahan on Qeshm Island, shops were open but the aisles were largely empty. A fuel tank exploded in Tehran. Officials said the cause was under investigation.

Iran also announced the execution of a foreign national, Qassem Hosseini, convicted of taking part in anti-government unrest in Isfahan.

The state says it is preparing stronger weapons, a new regional order, and a response outside the nuclear treaty. It is also managing fuel lines, empty markets, unexplained explosions, and the public mood that comes with them.
